title: When should I start talking to kids about money?
content: ## **When to Talk to Kids About Money!** Here's a secret: you're already talking to your children about money. And so is the world. The difference is that much of the teaching parents do isn't intentional, unlike the messages children receive from advertisers, marketers, and social media influencers. And they aren't the only ones talking to children about money. Family members, friends, neighbors, peers, teachers, and community leaders all play a role. While their intentions are often good, they may not be well versed in basic money principles or familiar with your family's values, goals, and priorities. This lack of intentionality, combined with the influence of outside voices, is a serious problem. It can undermine a child's long-term well-being—financial and otherwise—and limit future opportunities. **Parents Need to Know** Research, experience, and results all point to the same conclusion, **you cannot start your child's financial education too early.** The University of Cambridge found that adult money habits are largely formed by age seven. What's especially important to understand is that these habits become deeply ingrained over time. They are shaped less by logic and careful decision-making than by feelings, attitudes, and repeated behaviors influenced by the people and messages surrounding us. In other words, many of the money choices we make throughout our lives are not primarily driven by our values, goals, or long-term interests. Instead, they are often guided by feelings and attitudes formed in early childhood—sometimes by people and influences that do not necessarily have our best interests in mind. Take a moment to let that sink in. **Take Charge of Your Child's Financial Education** What it means is the years between ages three and seven represent a critical window of opportunity to take charge of your child's financial education and set them on a path toward lifelong financial well-being, confidence, security, and opportunity. So **start today**. Step by step, conversation by conversation, experience by experience, slowly and consistently begin addressing the challenge and helping children build a foundation for financial freedom, security, and opportunity. You can do it by intentionally talking to them about—and teaching them 7 of the most basic and life transforming money habits: (1) Saving, which means they will learn to delay gratification. It must be a priority if they are to have sustained and growing financial success. (2) Developing a strong work and earning ethic. (3) Spending smart, which means living on less than you earn. (4) Giving wisely and helping others. (5) Setting meaningful goals for your money. This means taking your time to figure out what you really want. (6) Planning and tracking your money (budgeting). (7) Learning to invest and grow your money, including understanding the power of compound interest. These simple habits, practiced consistently over time, can profoundly shape a child's future and reliably put them on a path toward greater confidence, independence, and financial well-being. **Grow Good Daily** At Grow Good Daily, we believe that intentional, tiny steps rooted in time-tested principles that are practiced consistently become habits that lead to larger-than-expected results over time. Financial education can and should be fun. And, it doesn't need to always be a formal lesson. It can be woven into everyday moments at home, in the grocery store, at the gas pump, during family outings, on birthdays, and around the dinner table. It can be one sentence or longer as you determine appropriate. Make deposits into a piggy bank, savings jar, or savings account a source of pride and accomplishment. You don't need to be a financial expert to raise a financially confident child. You simply need to be intentional, consistent, and present. Remember, children and young adults who never learned to save, budget, delay gratification, or distinguish needs from wants don't suddenly develop those skills at age 18 or 22. Too often, they struggle with debt, impulse spending, financial stress, and anxiety about money that can persist for years. Start now—wherever your child is and wherever you are. Because the best time to start was yesterday.
